samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A is the better deck: every title states a conclusion, each slide carries one idea, and it explains both commissary and utilization in a sentence each. Answer B is thorough and fair to Option B, and its risks slide and gap list are strong, but a few of its titles are topic labels and it never defines utilization. Both state the ask early and stay with the supplied figures; A's dates and slack estimate rest on an assumed fall date, though it marks them as estimates. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): A states the ask on slide 1, keeps every number to the supplied figures or plain arithmetic ($113K/yr rent, about $85K of rent before Dunmore produces), and gives a thorough list of gaps to close. B has tighter assertion-style titles and a sharp 26%-vs-30% slide, but its ask doesn't appear until slide 2. B also adds an estimated August start date and about a month of slack that don't come from the supplied facts, though it does flag them as estimates. The two are close; A edges ahead because its numbers stay strictly within the supplied facts.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A's slide titles are conclusions, so reading only the titles tells the whole argument. Answer B uses labels like 'Title', 'The ask' and 'Two options'. Both put the ask up front and treat Option B fairly, and B's table spelling out the 4-point shortfall is especially clear. A defines both commissary and utilization plainly. B gets today's date slightly wrong ('late October') and calls the second shift 'faster', which the supplied facts don't say. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers put the ask up front, show fairly that +26% falls short of the ~30% needed, and keep the spoken script separate from the slides. B wins mainly on slide titles: each states a conclusion, so reading the titles alone tells the story, while A uses labels like 'The ask', 'Two options' and 'Growth and lost revenue'. B also defines utilization more precisely and lays out the timeline arithmetic clearly; A wrongly says today is late October.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers state the ask up front, use claim-style slide titles and fit 15 minutes. B treats Option B more precisely ('about 4 points short', while granting that it is cheaper and faster) and explains 'commissary' and 'utilization' clearly for the board members outside food. A is more careful with numbers: it flags the unsupported 90% threshold, while B states that threshold as fact and claims Dunmore gives 'room beyond 30%' without any capacity figure. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers state the ask on slide 1, keep to 7 slides, show that Option B's +26% falls short of the 30% needed, and leave a placeholder for Dunmore's missing capacity figure. B's titles read more like conclusions, it warns the user not to use the 'roughly 90%' threshold unless they can stand behind it, and its 3-year cost arithmetic is correct and fairly framed. A's script asserts that Dunmore 'gives us room beyond 30%' with no supporting figure. A explains utilization and commissary more clearly for the two board members outside food, but B's stricter handling of the numbers makes it slightly stronger overall.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both put the Oct 31 decision and the non-renewal consequence on the first slide, and neither relies on speaker notes. B is denser and more complete for someone reading alone: its options table and the impact of losing the tenant (leased acreage falling to about 84%) give the committee what it needs to decide. A's 'four numbers, large' page leans toward the sparse big-number style, and its third page mostly repeats the first. B's extra figures ($468/acre, 84%, 380 acres, 7%) are plain arithmetic it discloses, but '$470/acre' in the title next to '$468' in the table is slightly inconsistent. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers put the decision and its consequence first, write slides that can be read without a presenter, and avoid speaker notes. A is denser and more useful for a decision: it compares approving and not approving, and it gives the effect of non-renewal on occupancy. Every figure it works out is plain arithmetic, and it flags each one, though its 84% figure assumes the 310 acres are currently leased. B is cleaner and caught that the Oct 31 deadline had already passed. However, B repeats page 1 on page 3, and page 2 shows big numbers with less analysis.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): A puts the ask on the title slide and lays out the approve/decline choice in a table, so the deck works for a desk read without a presenter. It flags its derived figures and accurately notes that Oct 31, 2026 is a Saturday, though it misses that the deadline has already passed. B catches that the deadline has passed and also leads with the ask, but its pages lean on big-number visuals and placeholders and slightly overstate the tenant's position ('expected to renew', 'will not renew unless repaired'). | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both drafts put the decision first and work without a presenter. A puts the consequence of declining on its first slide, where B only shows it on its last slide. A also notices that the Oct 31 deadline has already passed in the current environment, while B only notes it falls on a Saturday. B is denser and more desk-friendly because of its tables, but A's earlier consequence and its catch on the deadline make it slightly more useful.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B's slides are a bit tighter: there's no repeated decision slide, slide 3 is denser, and it rightly suggests adding a management recommendation. But B's timing note is wrong for today's date (Nov 4). It treats Oct 31 as still ahead, when it has already passed. A catches this, and it is the most important pre-send problem, so A wins even though its slide 2 is sparser and slides 1 and 4 repeat each other. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both decks put the decision first, label every figure clearly and use only the supplied facts or correct arithmetic on them. B notices that today is Nov 4, so the Oct 31 deadline has already passed, and that is the most important thing to fix before sending. A's advice to ask for replies by Friday evening assumes the deadline is still ahead, so it misreads the timing. A's slide 3 does explain the vacancy risk more clearly, but B's decision-and-risk slide covers similar ground.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a single opening with no preamble and no invented statistics. A's raise-your-hand twist gets the audience involved right away and quietly makes them admit they've overstated their own flossing, which leads straight into the talk's theme. B describes a moment hygienists will recognize from the chair, but it's one long sentence that ends by announcing the topic, so it lands less sharply when spoken. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Each answer gives one spoken-sounding opening with no statistics and no preamble. A uses the exact chairside moment these hygienists know, the 'Great' that doesn't match the patient's face, although its closing clause briefly announces the topic. B is a clever interactive hook, but it turns the hygienists into patients rather than drawing on the question they ask every day, so it fits the brief a little less directly.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both give a single quoted opening with no statistics and no preamble, apart from the quotation marks. B is more spoken and interactive: it puts the audience in the patient's position on the very question they ask every day, and it does not announce the topic. A uses a vivid, recognizable moment, but its second half drifts into a standard 'today I want to talk about' announcement. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both replies give a single opening with no statistics and no preamble. A's two-question hand-raise works well for this room: it turns the floss question back on the hygienists and quietly makes the talk's point about self-reporting before anything is announced. B opens with a vivid, familiar moment (the bleeding gums), but it ends by announcing the topic ('today I want to talk about why'), which weakens it.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both give exactly one spoken opening with no statistics, preamble or offer to refine. B is a tighter hook: it asks the hygienists themselves whether they have ever overstated their flossing to their own dentist, so the room feels the talk's point before it starts. A's bleeding gumline and mirror are vivid and clinical, but the 'sitting in this chair, with a mirror in my hand' wording leaves it unclear who is in the chair, which weakens the punchline. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a single opening, with no statistics and no preamble. A turns the question around neatly: hygienists are asked whether they have ever told their own dentist they floss daily, which leads straight into the talk's theme of why patients say it when it isn't true. B is more vivid, but its 'sitting in this chair, with a mirror in my hand' setup is hard to follow from a podium, and it is less clear who is the patient and who is the clinician.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend B right away, give reasons that fit the setting, and say specifically what is weak in A and C. Answer B is a little tighter. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick B right away, explain specifically why A and C are weaker, and stay short without rewriting the speech. A ties its reasons a bit more closely to this meeting, since council members hear many speakers who open with credentials and general claims. Its accuracy check is also more careful: it asks for the family's okay if they could be identified, and it names a fallback opening built on Alder's crash statistics. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick option B right away and say clearly what is weak in A and C. Answer B ties its reasons more closely to this meeting: council members hear many speakers open with credentials, and they can wave off national claims as not applying to their town. It also states the specific ask straight after the hook and gives a fallback if the story can't be used. Answer A leaves the specific ask until the end of the speech and treats getting the family's okay as optional ('if possible').

B wins because it puts the decision up front by retitling the opening slide as the ask, then keeps the ask slide on screen during questions; A saves the ask for the end. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B gives a firm, ordered list of 9 slides. It opens and closes on the ask, gives a reason for every cut, and names the likely Q&A topics (security, alternatives). A is tighter and better on assumptions and risk, especially its warning about weak adoption. However, it hedges between slides 10 and 12, and its timing doesn't add up: six slides at two minutes each is 12 minutes. B's count is also tight for 7 minutes of talking, but its plan is more decisive overall. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers open with the ask, cut the background slides with clear reasons and move the rest to an appendix. A gives a cleaner, unambiguous 9-slide order, while B contradicts itself (it says 5 content slides but lists 6) and leaves 10 vs 12 as an either-or. B edges ahead because it frames the decision more sharply, with claim titles and the amount, owner and date on the ask. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A gives a tight 7-slide deck that opens on the ask and comes back to it at the end. Its appendix is organized around the questions the committee is likely to ask, and it adds a fallback plan for losing more time and a specific warning about the soft staff-time estimate. Answer B is solid and its cuts are well reasoned, but it squeezes 10 slides into 10 minutes, leaves the ask slide at the end (only a verbal tip moves it forward), and its fallback tip refers to slides by their new position rather than their original number, which is confusing. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B builds the deck around the decision: it opens on the ask, gives a short 7-slide sequence, and arranges the appendix by the questions the committee is likely to ask. A has a solid 10-slide list and good backup slides, but it keeps the ask as the last slide and only moves it forward through a speaking tip. A's fallback advice also numbers slides by their new deck position, which is easy to confuse with the original slide numbers.
